name: Dull Red
lede: Dull Red is a descriptive name, a red with the shine taken out, and the books use it as a plain adjective phrase more than as the name of any one dye or pigment.

sections.title: A phrase, not a pigment
sections.body:
The books use "dull red" as everyday description. A painter's guide describes sunset skies as running from blue overhead to soft yellows and dull reds at the horizon [1]. Gage notes that Schoenberg's stage piece Die glückliche Hand calls for lights changing from dull red to yellow, through dirty green, violet, blue-grey and blood red [2]. No book treats it as a defined color with a recipe, so what it names is a loose range of reds rather than one shade.

The swatch here is a single screen sample of that range, not a reconstruction of anything historical.

sections.title: Hematite and dull-red heat
sections.body: Two technical uses are more exact. The pigment reference describes the common iron ore hematite as often a dull red, usually found as a crust in a rounded, kidney-like form [3]. The same source gives a recipe for a purple pigment, mineral lake, in which tin and chromium oxides are heated to "dull-red heat", a furnace temperature judged by the glow [4]. In both, the phrase is a working description rather than a name [3][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive the swatch matches 152 paintings out of 23,781 (0.64%, as photographed), more common than 66% of the named colors [5]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 1.8% of the 945 paintings from that century, about twice the rate expected from the same museums [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 90% of the 153 paintings that hold it [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test.

origin.named_after: origin undocumented; a plain descriptive phrase
